question.text: A trader notices that the put-call parity relationship is violated in the market: C - P is significantly greater than S - PV(K) for exchange-traded European IROs. What action can the trader take?

answer.text: Sell the call, buy the put, buy the underlying bond, and borrow PV(K) to earn a riskless arbitrage profit
Buy the call and sell the put to profit from the mispricing
Wait for the market to correct itself, as arbitrage is not possible in exchange-traded markets
Report the discrepancy to the exchange as a market manipulation

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook's put-call parity equation can be written as C + PV(K) = P + S. Rearranging gives C - P = S - PV(K). If the market price has C - P > S - PV(K), the left-hand "call + cash" side is overpriced relative to the right-hand "put + underlying" side. The trader sells the call (overpriced leg), buys the put, buys the underlying bond, and borrows PV(K) -- locking in the spread between the two sides. The Trap: Simply buying the call and selling the put doubles down on the mispricing rather than exploiting it. Arbitrage is possible in exchange-traded markets and is how parity is enforced. Note: In practice, transaction costs, bid-ask spreads, and execution frictions mean only sufficiently large parity deviations are profitable to arbitrage.
